claim: 96 Chinese and French 10-year-old children participated in the study, half of whom were struggling with reading.
source: In a cross-cultural paradigm, we measured the fMRI responses to words, faces, and houses in 96 Chinese and French 10-year-old children, half of whom were struggling with reading.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and confirmed in the methods section with specific group sizes.

claim: The reading circuit consists of the left fusiform gyrus, superior temporal gyrus/sulcus, precentral and middle frontal gyri.
source: We observed a reading circuit which was strikingly similar across languages and consisting of the left fusiform gyrus, superior temporal gyrus/sulcus, precentral and middle frontal gyri.
evidence: This finding is based on fMRI data analysis across all participants.

claim: Activations in some reading-related areas were modulated either by language or by reading ability, but without interaction between those factors.
source: Activations in some of these areas were modulated either by language or by reading ability, but without interaction between those factors.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of fMRI data showing main effects but no interaction.

claim: Reading difficulty affected activation similarly in Chinese and French readers in various regions previously associated with dyslexia, including the middle frontal gyrus.
source: In various regions previously associated with dyslexia, reading difficulty affected activation similarly in Chinese and French readers, including the middle frontal gyrus, a region previously described as specifically altered in Chinese.
evidence: This is based on ROI analysis showing main effects of reading ability without language interaction.

claim: The middle frontal gyrus was previously described as specifically altered in Chinese dyslexics.
source: including the middle frontal gyrus, a region previously described as specifically altered in Chinese.
evidence: This refers to prior literature on Chinese dyslexia.

claim: There is a large degree of cross-cultural invariance in the neural correlates of reading acquisition and reading impairment.
source: Our analyses reveal a large degree of cross-cultural invariance in the neural correlates of reading acquisition and reading impairment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of Chinese and French children.

claim: English may be considered an outlier within alphabetic writing systems due to its highly opaque grapheme-phoneme correspondences.
source: A large proportion of published studies on reading concern English, even though this language may be considered as an outlier within alphabetic writing systems, compared to Finnish or Italian for example, due to its highly opaque grapheme-phoneme correspondences.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about orthographic transparency.

claim: Daniels and Share (2018) listed 10 dimensions that might affect reading acquisition and dyslexia phenotypes.
source: Daniels and Share, 2018 listed 10 dimensions that might affect reading acquisition and dyslexia phenotypes, and that fall into three main classes: the structure of the oral language, the complexity of the visual shapes, and the translation rules between those two domains.
evidence: This is a direct reference to a published work.

claim: Orthographic transparency has been robustly reported to affect reading acquisition in Western languages.
source: All these factors may influence the speed and effectiveness with which children learn to read, and at least one of these dimensions, orthographic transparency, has been robustly reported to affect reading acquisition in Western languages (Seymour et al., 2003), with a reported impact on brain activation in the adult reading circuit (Paulesu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Orthographic transparency has a reported impact on brain activation in the adult reading circuit.
source: All these factors may influence the speed and effectiveness with which children learn to read, and at least one of these dimensions, orthographic transparency, has been robustly reported to affect reading acquisition in Western languages (Seymour et al., 2003), with a reported impact on brain activation in the adult reading circuit (Paulesu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paulesu et al., 2000.

claim: All writing systems comprise a restricted number of visual symbols whose combinations allow access to the spoken language network through vision.
source: Beyond these surface differences, the fundamental logic of reading remains the same from one writing system to another: all of them comprise a restricted number of visual symbols whose combinations allow to access the spoken language network through vision.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of writing systems based on established knowledge.

claim: Grapheme-phoneme correspondences depend on a precise region of the visual system, the visual word-form area (VWFA) and on the posterior superior temporal cortex.
source: Grapheme-phoneme correspondences are arbitrary and have been shown to depend on a precise region of the visual system, the visual word-form area (VWFA) and on the posterior superior temporal cortex, as shown by numerous brain imaging studies in adult readers (Baker et al., 2007; Dehaene et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to brain imaging studies.

claim: Most brain imaging studies on reading concern mainly Western alphabetic languages and mainly adults.
source: However, most of those brain imaging studies suffer from the bias noted above: they concern mainly Western alphabetic languages and mainly adults.
evidence: This is an observation about the literature based on review of existing studies.

claim: Chinese characters map onto phonology at the syllable level with a considerable degree of irregularity.
source: For instance, Chinese characters, like letters, eventually map onto phonology, but they do so at the syllable level and with a considerable degree of irregularity, with (in most cases) no parts in a character corresponding to phonological segments such as phonemes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Chinese orthography.

claim: Children may rely on different and possibly broader regions of the brain before converging onto the adult expert network for reading.
source: Children may rely on different and possibly broader regions of the brain before converging onto the adult expert network for reading, for instance transiently recruiting parietal regions for effortful reading (Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuroimaging studies of dyslexia have revealed common neural deficits in different alphabetic languages, with consistently decreased activation in several left-hemispheric posterior regions.
source: Neuroimaging studies of dyslexia have revealed common neural deficits in different alphabetic languages, with consistently decreased activation (Martin et al., 2016; Richlan et al., 2009) and reduced gray-matter volumes (Linkersdörfer et al., 2012; Richlan et al., 2013) in several left-hemispheric posterior regions, including the left temporoparietal and left ventral occipitotemporal regions.
evidence: This is based on multiple meta-analyses cited.

claim: The left ventral posterior occipitotemporal cortex (including the Visual Word-Form Area, VWFA) is the most reproducible and consistent site exhibiting hypoactivation in dyslexic individuals across several alphabetic writing systems.
source: According to two recent meta-analyses, the left ventral posterior occipitotemporal cortex (including the Visual Word-Form Area, VWFA) appears to be the most reproducible and consistent site exhibiting hypoactivation in dyslexic individuals across several alphabetic writing systems regardless of orthographic depth (Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on meta-analyses cited.

claim: Chinese dyslexic children showed decreased activation in the left middle frontal gyrus (LMFG) compared with typical readers during a homophone judgment task.
source: Chinese dyslexic children showed a decreased activation in the LMFG compared with typical readers (with eight 11-year-old children in each group) during a homophone judgment task (Siok et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a citation to a specific prior study.

claim: The decreased activation in the LMFG in Chinese dyslexics was associated with smaller gray-matter volume at the same location.
source: This decreased activation in the LMFG was replicated by Siok et al., 2008, with twelve 11-year-old children in each group. It was associated with smaller gray-matter volume at the same location, and no other functional or structural differences was found in the regions singled out by other studies in alphabetic languages.
evidence: This is a citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Behavioral data show similar profiles in Chinese and alphabetic-language dyslexics.
source: However, these findings contradict behavioral data that show similar profiles in Chinese and alphabetic-language dyslexics (Goswami et al., 2011; Ziegler and Goswami, 2005) and similar predictors of reading abilities in both writing systems.
evidence: This is based on citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Phonological awareness and morphological awareness in 4-year-old Chinese children predict character recognition at 11 years of age.
source: For instance, phonological awareness and morphological awareness (lexical compounding) in 4-year-old Chinese children predict character recognition at 11 years of age, while naming speed (RAN) and vocabulary predict reading fluency (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on a longitudinal study cited.

claim: Naming speed (RAN) and vocabulary predict reading fluency in Chinese children.
source: For instance, phonological awareness and morphological awareness (lexical compounding) in 4-year-old Chinese children predict character recognition at 11 years of age, while naming speed (RAN) and vocabulary predict reading fluency (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on a longitudinal study cited.

claim: In alphabetic languages, phonological awareness is linked to reading accuracy and RAN to reading fluency.
source: These results are consistent with those obtained in alphabetic languages, which link phonological awareness to reading accuracy and RAN to reading fluency (Landerl et al., 2013; Moll et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on citations to studies in alphabetic languages.

claim: An fMRI study revealed remarkably few differences in brain activity between 11 English and 11 Chinese dyslexic adolescents once confounding variables were controlled for.
source: Moreover, another fMRI study revealed remarkably few differences in brain activity between 11 English and 11 Chinese dyslexic adolescents (13 to 16 years) once all confounding variables (e.g. stimuli and task in fMRI) were controlled for (Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation to a specific comparative study.

claim: The study included 96 Chinese and French 10-year-old readers (48 in each language), with different reading proficiency.
source: Therefore, to clarify the question of the commonalities and specificities of reading acquisition across different writing systems, we used a similar experimental protocol in 96 Chinese and French 10-year-old readers (48 in each language), with different reading proficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the methods description.

claim: Half of the children had reading difficulties, meeting the criteria for dyslexia in French children (more than 2 years of reading delay) though not as marked in Chinese children.
source: Half of the children had reading difficulties, meeting the criteria for dyslexia in French children (more than 2 years of reading delay) though not as marked in Chinese children. (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Table 1.

claim: All children performed the same passive viewing task with words, faces, and houses, with the goal to detect an occasional target star.
source: As in our previously published fMRI studies of reading (Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2018; Monzalvo and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2013), all children performed the same passive viewing task with words, faces, and houses, with the mere goal to detect an occasional target star.
evidence: This describes the experimental task used.

claim: Chinese children responded faster to the target star than French children.
source: Within the scanner, Chinese children responded faster to the target star than French children (main effect of Language: F (1,92)=60.94, p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data analysis.

claim: There was no significant effect of Reading ability on response time to the target star.
source: There was no significant effect of Reading ability (F (1,92)<1) nor Language × Reading ability interaction (F (1,92)<1)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The [Words > Faces + Houses] analysis yielded the usual reading-related regions: fusiform gyrus, posterior superior temporal region, planum temporale, intra-parietal sulcus and inferior frontal regions in the left hemisphere and the posterior superior temporal gyrus in the right hemisphere.
source: The [Words > Faces + Houses] analysis yielded the usual reading-related regions: fusiform gyrus, posterior superior temporal region, planum temporale, intra-parietal sulcus and inferior frontal regions in the left hemisphere and the posterior superior temporal gyrus in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is based on whole-brain fMRI analysis.

claim: The left VWFA was not seen in both Chinese and French poor readers at the classical threshold, contrary to typical readers.
source: Those results were seen in each of the four groups of subjects, with the interesting exception that the left VWFA was not seen in both Chinese and French poor readers, contrary to the typical readers, at this classical threshold (voxel-level p<0.001, cluster-level uncorrected) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on group-level fMRI analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reading scores across all 96 children were significantly correlated with fMRI activation in the [words > fixation] contrast in classical regions of the reading circuit in the left hemisphere plus some of their right counterparts.
source: Reading scores across all 96 children were significantly correlated with fMRI activation in the [words > fixation] contrast, in the classical regions of the reading circuit in the left hemisphere (fusiform, superior temporal sulcus, middle frontal region and precentral) plus some of their right counterparts (Figure 2 and Table 3).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2 and Table 3.

claim: A significant positive correlation was observed across all children between reading scores and face-evoked activation in the left fusiform gyrus.
source: We also observed a significant positive correlation, across all children, between reading scores and the face-evoked activation (vs fixation) in the left fusiform gyrus (left [−33 −60 −15], 74 voxels, Z = 4.31, pFWE_corr = 0.001).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of fMRI data.

claim: No significant difference was found between typical and poor readers in either direction when analyzing either the [Words > fixation] or the [Words > Faces+Houses] contrast across the whole brain.
source: No significant difference was found between typical and poor readers in either direction when analyzing either the [Words > fixation] or the [Words > Faces+Houses] contrast across the whole brain.
evidence: This is based on whole-brain statistical analysis.

claim: Typical readers showed larger activations relative to poor readers in a left precentral cluster within reading sensitive regions.
source: Typical readers showed larger activations relative to poor readers in a left precentral cluster (79 voxels, pFWE_corr = 0.027, Z = 3.69 at [−51 15 33])
evidence: This is based on ROI analysis within a mask of word-specific voxels.

claim: Chinese children showed larger activation relative to French children in the left intra-parietal sulcus within reading sensitive regions.
source: and Chinese relative to French in the left intra-parietal sulcus (55 voxels, pFWE_corr = 0.004, Z = 4.29 at [−30–60 39]) in the words vs. fixation contrast (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on ROI analysis within a mask of word-specific voxels.

claim: All ROIs (except two ROIs in the right hemisphere) from dyslexia meta-analyses fell within the reading circuit identified in the participants.
source: All ROIs (except two ROIs in the right hemisphere) fell within the reading circuit identified in our participants (Words > other categories; see Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of literature-derived ROIs with the study's activation maps.

claim: A significant main effect of Language was observed in the left middle frontal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, and posterior superior temporal gyrus, always due to larger activation in Chinese readers than in French readers.
source: A significant main effect of Language was observed in the left middle frontal gyrus (F (1,92)=15.23, p<0.001, pFDR_corr < 0.001), superior parietal lobule (SPL, F (1,92)=8.13, p=0.005, pFDR_corr = 0.022) and posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG, F (1,92)=9.04, p=0.003, pFDR_corr = 0.020), always due to larger activation in Chinese readers than in French readers (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of ROI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Significant reduced activation was observed in poor readers relative to typical readers in the left fusiform gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus.
source: Significant reduced activation was observed in poor readers relative to typical readers in the left fusiform gyrus (F(1,92) = 21.08, p<0.001, pFDR_corr < 0.001), middle frontal gyrus (F (1,92)=10.17, p=0.002, pFDR_corr = 0.009), superior temporal sulcus (F (1,92)=11.88, p=0.001, pFDR_corr = 0.006), and precentral gyrus (F (1,92)=7.78, p=0.006, pFDR_corr = 0.020).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of ROI data.

claim: No ROI showed a significant language × reading ability interaction.
source: No ROI showed a significant language × reading ability interaction (see Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), even the pSTG (F (1,92)=2.815, p=0.097 before FDR correction).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of ROI data.

claim: Bayesian analyses provided similar conclusions to frequentist analyses for the main effect of Language and Reading ability.
source: Bayesian analyses provided similar conclusions to frequentist analyses for the main effect of Language and Reading ability (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian statistical analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: There was strong evidence of a reading ability effect in the fusiform gyrus (FFG) and moderate evidence in the STS and PCG in both languages.
source: Notably, there was strong evidence of a reading ability effect in the fusiform gyrus (FFG) and moderate evidence in the STS and PCG in both languages.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian analysis with Bayes factors reported in Table 4.

claim: The Euclidean distance of individual centers of mass for word activations to the group peaks did not differ between poor and typical readers in left FFG, MFG, STS, PCG, SPL, and pSTG.
source: Considering the locations of the individual centers of mass for word activations in the left FFG, MFG, STS, PCG, SPL, pSTG, their Euclidean distance to the group peaks did not differ between poor and typical readers (Supplementary file 6), suggesting a similar dispersion among poor readers and typical readers.
evidence: This is based on individual peak location analysis.

claim: Even after selecting the best responding voxels in each child, word activation remained weaker in poor than typical readers in the left FFG, MFG, STS, PCG, and pSTG.
source: Furthermore, even after having selected the best responding voxels in each child, the word activation remained weaker in poor than typical readers in the left FFG, MFG, STS, PCG, and pSTG (all pFDR_corr < 0.05).
evidence: This is based on individual peak activation analysis.

claim: In all the ROIs, there was an overall replicable pattern of activation evoked by words, as indicated by a significant main effect of condition in MVPA analysis.
source: In all the ROIs, when pooling over all subjects, there was an overall replicable pattern of activation evoked by words, as indicated by a significant main effect of condition, with a greater correlation coefficient within words than between words and other categories (all pFDR_corr < 0.001) (see Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on MVPA analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significant interaction of condition × reading ability was observed in the left FFG and left pSTG in MVPA analysis.
source: Crucially, we also observed a significant interaction of condition × reading ability (typical vs. poor readers) in the left FFG (F (1, 83)=10.14, p=0.002, pFDR_corr = 0.006) and in the left pSTG (F (1, 83)=15.75, p<0.001, pFDR_corr < 0.001).
evidence: This is based on MVPA analysis.

claim: Typical readers, but not poor readers, exhibited a significantly similar pattern of activation from one run to the next in the left FFG and pSTG.
source: Post-hoc analysis found that typical readers, but not poor readers, exhibited a significantly similar pattern of activation from one run to the next.
evidence: This is based on post-hoc analysis of MVPA results.

claim: Children struggling with reading acquisition exhibited a genuinely more erratic activation pattern for words in the FFG and pSTG regions.
source: Those results show that the above differences between typical and poor readers were not due to an artifact of group averaging, and that children struggling with reading acquisition exhibited a genuinely more erratic activation pattern for words in these regions (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MVPA results shown in Figure 5.

claim: For the bilateral fusiform face areas, only the main effect of condition reached significance in MVPA analysis, with no effect of reading ability.
source: For the MVPA analysis in the bilateral fusiform face areas (bilateral FFA), only the main effect of condition reached significance (pFDR_corr < 0.001), with a greater correlation coefficient for within-category patterns (faces-faces) than for between-category patterns (faces-words, faces-houses, words-houses). Neither the main effect of reading ability nor the interaction of condition × reading ability reached significance.
evidence: This is based on MVPA analysis of face responses.

claim: Chinese children had greater response to words in the right hemisphere compared to French children at several y coordinates along the anterior-posterior gradient.
source: Firstly, we observed greater response to words in Chinese children compared to French children in the right hemisphere at several y coordinates, leading to a significant triple interaction of language × hemisphere × ROI.
evidence: This is based on analysis of anterior-posterior gradient in ventral temporal cortex.

claim: Poor readers had weaker activation to words at several consecutive sites (y-axis at −64, −55, −46, and −37) compared to typical readers.
source: Crucially, the reading ability × ROIs interaction was significant. In more detail, compared to typical readers, poor readers had weaker activation to words at several consecutive sites (y-axis at −64, −55, −46, and −37).
evidence: This is based on analysis of anterior-posterior gradient.

claim: Both Chinese and French poor readers have significantly lower activations relative to their controls at y = −46, corresponding to the classical coordinates of the VWFA.
source: However, when we considered separately Chinese and French children, only one site (y = −46) survived correction for multiple comparison in both Chinese and French children. This site is only slightly anterior to the classic VWFA site (Cohen et al., 2002) (see Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 6B with citation to the classic VWFA coordinates.

claim: The main effect of reading ability on face activation reached significance, due to lower activation to faces in poor readers compared to typical readers bilaterally and in both languages.
source: Besides, the main effect of reading ability reached significance, due to a lower activation to faces in poor readers compared to typical readers bilaterally and in both languages (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of face responses along the anterior-posterior gradient shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Learning to read largely involves the same key regions across cultures and ages, but with quantitative modulations depending on the specific demands of the task, the learning stage, and culture-dependent characteristics.
source: Overall, our findings indicate that learning to read largely involves the same key regions across cultures and ages, but with quantitative modulations depending on the specific demands of the task, the learning stage, and culture-dependent characteristics.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the overall results.

claim: The greater involvement of the left intraparietal sulcus in Chinese reading is presumably due to the greater amount of spatial analysis required by Chinese character recognition.
source: We therefore speculate that the greater involvement of this region in Chinese reading is presumably due to the greater amount of spatial analysis required by Chinese character recognition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed difference.

claim: The left intraparietal sulcus plays a role in visuo-spatial encoding and attention, including the serial analysis of letters in a word or pseudoword.
source: Brain imaging research has well documented the role of the left intraparietal sulcus in visuo-spatial encoding and attention (Davranche et al., 2011; Offen et al., 2010), including the serial analysis of letters in a word or pseudoword (Cohen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior brain imaging research.

claim: The most likely explanation for LMFG involvement is that it is systematically involved in writing.
source: Perhaps the most likely explanation is that the LMFG, as well as the more medial and dorsal Exner area, are systematically involved in writing (Planton et al., 2013; Purcell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on citations to prior research on writing.

claim: The left MFG includes a representation of handwriting gestures that is engaged in both alphabetical and non-alphabetical languages.
source: FMRI studies in typical adult readers, comparing French and Chinese reading, have shown that the left MFG is not specific to Chinese writing, but includes a representation of handwriting gestures that is engaged in both alphabetical and non-alphabetical languages (Nakamura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a comparative fMRI study.

claim: Writing facilitates reading acquisition in children.
source: Furthermore, writing is not only learned in parallel with reading, but facilitates reading acquisition in children (Bara et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: The greater activation in the right ventral visual system in Chinese reading has been reported in previous literature and shows a children-to-adult developmental increase.
source: The greater activation in the right ventral visual system in Chinese reading has been reported in previous literature and this region has been found to show a children-to-adult developmental increase for Chinese, suggesting that this region is especially important in Chinese reading acquisition, presumably because of its involvement of holistic visuo-orthographic processes (Bolger et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior literature with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The posterior superior temporal gyrus/sulcus is associated with phonological processing and grapheme-phoneme conversion.
source: This region is associated with phonological processing and grapheme-phoneme conversion (Turkeltaub et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: Chinese readers must rely more heavily on the direct route from orthography to the lexicon because phonological information is insufficient to access semantics of a printed character.
source: In Chinese reading, a large number of written characters correspond to the same syllable, thus phonological information is insufficient to access semantics of a printed character. As a result, Chinese readers must rely more heavily on the direct route from orthography to the lexicon (Cao et al., 2010; Shu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior research on Chinese reading.

claim: Phoneme-level representation plays an essential role in learning to read Chinese, especially in beginners who rely on Pinyin.
source: However, phoneme-level representation still plays an essential role in learning to read Chinese, all the more that syllable decoding is complex. This may be especially true in beginners, who rely on Pinyin, an alphabetic notation which allows children to manipulate different phonological units such as decomposing a syllable into onset, rime, tone and phonemes.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about Chinese reading instruction.

claim: The reduced activations in poor readers are not an artifact of group averaging solely due to greater inter-individual variability in the localization of reading-related circuits in the dyslexic brain.
source: Thanks to individual peak location and intensity analyses, as well as multivariate pattern analyses, we could reject an alternative interpretation which, to the best of our knowledge, was not explicitly tested in previous studies: the possibility that the reduced activations are an artifact of group averaging, solely due to greater inter-individual variability in the localization of reading-related circuits in the dyslexic brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the individual analyses performed.

claim: The reduced activation to written words may not reflect a general disorganization of the extra-striate visual areas, but rather a specific difficulty with written words.
source: This observation suggests that the reduced activation to written words may not reflect a general disorganization of the extra-striate visual areas, but rather a specific difficulty with written words.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MVPA results showing stable face responses but unstable word responses in poor readers.

claim: The under-activation of the VWFA in poor readers may simply reflect the lack of reading practice and might be a consequence rather than a cause of the reading deficit.
source: Given that the site of the VWFA does not activate strongly to written words in illiterates (Dehaene et al., 2010; Hervais-Adelman et al., 2019) and in typical children before they learn to read (Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2018), its under-activation in poor readers may simply reflect the lack of reading practice – in other words, it might be a consequence rather than a cause of the reading deficit.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on citations to prior research.

claim: Dyslexia is likely to be a heterogeneous deficit with a variety of different causes.
source: Dyslexia is likely to be a heterogeneous deficit with a variety of different causes, including a phonological deficit in many children, but also visual attentional deficits, plausibly anywhere along the complex processing chain that leads from print to sound and meaning (Friedmann et al., 2010; Paulesu et al., 2014; Valdois et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior research on dyslexia.

claim: A reduced activation in the VWFA is one of the dominant fMRI signatures of reading poor performances.
source: The present study cannot distinguish cause from consequence, but it does demonstrate that a reduced activation in the VWFA is one of the dominant fMRI signatures of reading poor performances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The left posterior STG is involved in grapheme-phoneme conversion.
source: The other major site of atypical activation reported in the dyslexia literature is the left posterior STG, a region involved in grapheme-phoneme conversion (Frost et al., 2009; Turkeltaub et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on citations to prior research.

claim: The left posterior STG location is less consistently found in children than in adults in dyslexia studies.
source: although this location is less consistently found in children than in adults (Richlan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The left posterior STG is under-activated during spoken language processing in illiterates and in preliterate children compared to adult and children readers.
source: Again, because this site is also under-activated during spoken language processing in illiterates and in preliterate children compared to adult and children readers (Dehaene et al., 2010)
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: Phonological awareness is both a predictor of future reading and a consequence of learning to read in an alphabetical language.
source: Indeed, it does not have to be one or the other, but could be both, as phonological awareness is known to be both a predictor of future reading (Hulme et al., 2012; Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012), and a consequence of learning to read in an alphabetical language (Morais et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior research.

claim: Atypical activation in the left middle frontal gyrus is not unique to Chinese poor readers, but can be found in alphabetic readers as well and is part of a universal phenotype of reading disability.
source: While a null effect can never be firmly asserted, the present results positively indicate that atypical activation in this region is not unique to Chinese poor readers, but can be found in alphabetic readers as well and is therefore part of a universal phenotype of reading disability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Chinese readers may rely more on a motor memory of writing gestures as a means for memorizing the large number of characters.
source: To overcome this difficulty, Chinese readers may rely more on a motor memory of writing gestures as a means for memorizing the large number of characters, and as noted earlier, writing skills predict reading ability in Chinese children (Tan et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on a citation.

claim: The dysfunction of the left MFG in Chinese poor readers may reflect an underlying deficit in memorizing writing gestures.
source: The greater activation of the left MFG may therefore reflect the greater reliance of Chinese children on writing, and the dysfunction of this region in Chinese poor readers may reflect an underlying deficit in memorizing writing gestures (Ziegler, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on a citation.

claim: Novice readers in alphabetic languages benefit from a motor memory for hand gestures when recognizing written words.
source: This strategy is not unique to Chinese, however: novice readers in alphabetic languages also benefit from a motor memory for hand gestures when recognizing written words (Bara et al., 2004)
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: A motor representation of handwriting gestures is automatically accessed for subliminal written words in both Chinese and French adult readers.
source: and a recent study found that a motor representation of handwriting gestures is automatically accessed for subliminal written words in both Chinese and French adult readers (Nakamura et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a specific study.

claim: The left MFG is likely to play a pivotal role in successful reading acquisition independently of the writing system.
source: Our findings on children further suggest that the left MFG is likely to play a pivotal role in successful reading acquisition independently of the writing system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The task was orthogonal to reading and involved the mere detection of a picture of a star to avoid any effect due to performance differences.
source: First, our task was orthogonal to reading, and involved the mere detection of a picture of a star. This choice was made to avoid any effect due to performance itself.
evidence: This describes the methodological choice made in the study.

claim: The reading delay in Chinese children was less than in French children.
